rows.notes: The paper is a 'Case Report' that self-describes its method (Section 3) as an extensive literature review and analysis of existing data on the Lower Indus; its waterlogging, salinity, water-table and crop-yield figures are drawn from WAPDA/IWASRI/consultant reports (refs 1, 3, 8, 18) rather than from any experiment, survey or model of the authors. It is a synthesis/policy piece, so Q1 is 'no'. Even if treated as primary, it contains no result on drip or micro-irrigation: micro-irrigation is only listed (Section 6.1) as one of several recommended water-saving techniques to accompany reduced canal supplies. What the paper actually argues is that reduced surface canal allocations (drought years 1999-2002, LBOD drainage, private tube-well pumping) lowered water tables and reduced waterlogging/salinity without reducing yields; the technology is canal reallocation/conjunctive groundwater use, not drip.

Same study: a literature-review/case report synthesising secondary data (Section 3), not a primary study, so Q1 is 'no'. It does not examine micro-irrigation's effect on groundwater recharge at all. The groundwater balance it presents (Table 4, from Halcrow-ACE 2003) attributes recharge to canal seepage and irrigation return flow and says 74%-80% of recharge is lost to non-beneficial evaporation; the paper argues recharge/water tables should be lowered via rationalised canal duties and groundwater pumping. Micro-irrigation appears only as a recommendation (Section 6.1), with no reported effect on recharge.

notes: Full text appears complete. The paper is a policy-oriented case report on conjunctive surface/groundwater management in Sindh; it never studies drip/micro-irrigation, so it cannot provide own evidence for either claim. The review's citation attributes to it claims about micro-irrigation that the paper does not make from its own findings.
